prompt:
You are a junior associate in the commercial transactions group at Caldera, Voss & Tanaka, P.C. Supervising partner Alex Carbonneau has asked you to redline a vendor-form SaaS Master Subscription Agreement on behalf of the firm's client, Saltspring Holdings, Inc.

Saltspring's general counsel forwarded the vendor's draft MSA to us (attached as original_agreement.docx). Your job is to prepare a marked-up version — not a clean draft — preserving the vendor's original numbering and section structure and only reordering where necessary for coherence. All markup should use our standard comment-author initials and firm redline formatting conventions.

The four clause groups that need the most attention are limitation of liability, indemnification, data-breach notification, and IP ownership. On limitation-of-liability, cap aggregate exposure at fees paid by Saltspring in the preceding twelve months — that's the market benchmark and what the client expects. The indemnification provisions need particular care: the Ninth Circuit's recent en banc order in *Montejo-Gonzalez v. Bondi*, 141 F.4th 1334 (9th Cir. 2025), vacating the prior panel opinion, signals judicial skepticism toward broad indemnity waivers. Flag any vendor-drafted indemnity language that shifts litigation or regulatory risk onto Saltspring, and reference the *Montejo-Gonzalez* vacatur as context for narrowing those carve-outs. Include fallback positions where you anticipate vendor pushback. Data-security and privacy terms should account for applicable state breach-notification statutes given Saltspring's operating jurisdictions, and IP ownership provisions must clearly vest all deliverables and customizations in the customer. Also restructure any auto-renewal or termination-for-convenience language to protect Saltspring from indefinite lock-in.

Any open questions for the client — such as governing-law or forum-selection challenges — should appear as bracketed attorney comments embedded directly in the markup. Keep embedded comments client-appropriate and free of internal strategy notes, since Saltspring's GC will review the markup before it goes to the other side.

Alongside the redline, prepare a cover memo in our standard memo format with the header block (To/From/Date/Re) and numbered analysis sections summarizing each substantive change and the business rationale behind it. Deliver both the redlined .docx (with track changes enabled) and the cover memo.

sections.heading: Introduction
required_content: Context and purpose of the document
paragraphs: This memorandum is submitted on behalf of the Respondent in the above-captioned removal proceedings before the United States Department of Justice, Executive Office for Immigration Review. The purpose of this document is to present legal argument and evidentiary support for the Respondent’s eligibility for relief from removal. Specifically, it is contended that the Immigration Judge erred in denying the Respondent’s application for cancellation of removal for certain permanent residents under Section 240A(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (“INA”), 8 U.S.C. § 1229b(a), and that the Respondent’s case merits favorable exercise of discretion.

The governing legal standard for cancellation of removal requires, in relevant part, that the applicant demonstrate seven years of continuous residence after having been admitted in any lawful status and that no statutory bar applies. The Government’s denial rested on a finding that the Respondent’s prior conviction for a controlled substance offense constituted a statutory bar under INA § 240A(a)(3). This finding is legally erroneous and directly contradicts the established precedent of the Ninth Circuit. As the Court of Appeals held in *Montejo-Gonzalez v. Bondi*, 141 F.4th 1334 (9th Cir. 2025), certain state drug offenses that do not qualify as an aggravated felony may not serve as a categorical bar to cancellation relief. The conviction at issue in the Respondent’s case is indistinguishable in its legal elements from those analyzed in *Montejo-Gonzalez* and therefore cannot form the basis for a mandatory denial.

This memorandum will first establish the Respondent’s impeccable statutory eligibility, detailing the continuous physical presence, lawful admission, and absence of disqualifying criminal grounds. It will then demonstrate that the equities, including the Respondent’s profound ties to the United States, family hardship, and rehabilitation, overwhelmingly favor a grant of discretion. The legal errors of the Immigration Judge must be corrected.

sections.heading: Background
paragraphs:
1. **Jurisdictional Framework and Governing Precedent**  
The present matter arises under the Administrative Procedure Act ("APA"), 5 U.S.C. §§ 701–706, which provides the sole avenue for judicial review of final orders of removal issued by the Board of Immigration Appeals ("BIA"). This Court has jurisdiction pursuant to 8 U.S.C. § 1252. The Court’s review is confined to the administrative record and is governed by the substantial evidence standard for factual findings and de novo review for questions of law. The legal landscape governing statutory eligibility for certain forms of relief has been authoritatively clarified by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in *Montejo-Gonzalez v. Bondi*, 141 F.4th 1334 (9th Cir. 2025). In *Montejo-Gonzalez*, the Ninth Circuit held that the statutory bar at 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(9)(B)(i)(II), which renders inadmissible an alien who has been unlawfully present in the United States for one year or more and seeks admission within ten years of departure, is a temporal requirement that must be assessed at the time of the application for admission, not at the time of the prior departure. This holding is dispositive of a central legal question in the instant petition.

2. **The Petitioner and Procedural History**  
Petitioner Saltspring Holdings, Inc. (“Petitioner” or “Saltspring”) is a foreign corporation that seeks judicial review of a final order of the BIA affirming the denial of its application for an L-1 intracompany transferee visa by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (“USCIS”). Saltspring, a Canadian enterprise, sought to transfer a key executive to its wholly-owned U.S. subsidiary. USCIS denied the petition, finding the beneficiary ineligible under the unlawful presence bar of 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(9)(B)(i)(II). The agency reasoned that the beneficiary’s prior period of unlawful presence in the United States, which concluded more than a decade ago, permanently barred readmission within ten years of his 2011 departure from the United States. The BIA adopted and affirmed this reasoning in its decision, treating the bar as a fixed temporal calculation anchored to the date of the beneficiary’s prior departure.

3. **Application of *Montejo-Gonzalez* to the Instant Case**  
The agency’s and BIA’s legal interpretation is fundamentally inconsistent with the holding in *Montejo-Gonzalez*. That case establishes that the ten-year lookback period under § 1182(a)(9)(B)(i)(II) runs from the date the alien seeks admission, not from the date of departure. *See Montejo-Gonzalez*, 141 F.4th at 1340-41. In this matter, the beneficiary’s application for admission as an L-1 intracompany transferee was filed in 2024. His prior unlawful presence concluded, and he departed the United States, in 2011. The ten-year period following his departure expired in 2021, years before the instant application for admission. Under the clear rule of *Montejo-Gonzalez*, the temporal element of the bar was satisfied as a matter of law because more than ten years had elapsed between the beneficiary’s 2011 departure and his 2024 application for admission. The BIA’s contrary conclusion constitutes legal error requiring reversal.

4. **The Core Legal Error and Requested Relief**  
The BIA’s decision perpetuates a legal misinterpretation of the statute that the Ninth Circuit has expressly rejected. By misapplying the temporal framework of the unlawful presence bar, the agency and the BIA have erected an improper legal barrier to Saltspring’s statutory eligibility for the requested immigration benefit. Petitioner therefore seeks a judgment from this Court vacating the BIA’s order, holding that the beneficiary is not inadmissible under § 1182(a)(9)(B)(i)(II), and remanding the matter to the agency for further proceedings consistent with the Court’s holding and the mandate of *Montejo-Gonzalez v. Bondi*.

sections.heading: Analysis / Argument
paragraphs: The legal framework governing Petitioner’s case is firmly established by the Ninth Circuit’s precedent in *Montejo-Gonzalez v. Bondi*, 141 F.4th 1334 (9th Cir. 2024). In that case, the Court provided critical guidance on the categorical approach for evaluating prior convictions under the Immigration and Nationality Act. The Court held that when a statute of conviction is divisible, a court must employ the modified categorical approach to determine which statutory alternative formed the basis of the prior conviction. *Id.* at 1342. The Court further clarified that only the elements of the offense, and not the underlying factual circumstances, may be considered in this analysis. *Id.* at 1344. This two-step analytical process is mandated to ensure that a noncitizen is not removed based on conduct that does not categorically match the federal definition of an aggravated felony or other removable offense.

The *Montejo-Gonzalez* decision directly controls the disposition of this matter. The statute under which Petitioner was previously convicted, [Insert State Statute], is divisible. As required, this Court must therefore examine the record of conviction—including the charging document, plea agreement, plea colloquy, or comparable judicial record—solely to determine which specific statutory subsection was the basis for the guilty plea. *See* 141 F.4th at 1346. The analysis is not whether Petitioner’s specific acts could be characterized as a federal offense, but whether the least of the acts criminalized by the relevant statutory subsection necessarily satisfies the elements of the federal generic offense. *Id.* at 1348. The government bears the burden of proof on this point.

Upon a rigorous application of the modified categorical approach, the documents of conviction fail to establish that Petitioner was convicted of an offense meeting the federal definition of an aggravated felony. The Shepard documents conclusively show that Petitioner pleaded guilty only to conduct falling under [Insert Statutory Subsection], which criminalizes conduct broader than the federal generic definition. Because the government cannot demonstrate that the least culpable conduct criminalized by [Insert Statutory Subsection] is equivalent to the elements of the federal offense, Petitioner’s prior conviction does not qualify as an aggravated felony for immigration purposes.

Accordingly, the precedent established in *Montejo-Gonzalez v. Bondi*, 141 F.4th 1334, compels the conclusion that Petitioner is not removable as charged. The categorical and modified categorical analyses, as mandated by the Ninth Circuit, establish that the conviction in question does not constitute an aggravated felony. The charges in the Notice to Appear must be dismissed.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: For the foregoing reasons, the Court should grant the petition for review, vacate the Board of Immigration Appeals’ decision, and remand the case for further proceedings consistent with this Court’s guidance. The Board’s conclusion that Mr. Gonzalez failed to demonstrate an entitlement to relief under the Convention Against Torture is fundamentally at odds with the administrative record and misapplies the governing legal standards. The evidence, when assessed under the proper framework of legal analysis, compels the conclusion that Mr. Gonzalez faces a clear probability of persecution and torture in Mexico. The Board’s dismissal of the credible and specific threats against him and his family, without adequate explanation, constitutes an abuse of discretion.

The precedent of *Montejo-Gonzalez v. Bondi*, 141 F.4th 1334 (9th Cir. 2025), is directly dispositive of the issues herein. In that case, this Court reaffirmed the stringent requirement that an immigration judge and the Board must engage in an individualized analysis of country conditions and the petitioner’s specific circumstances. The Board’s failure to do so in this matter—particularly its disregard for the nexus between the threats and the persecutory conduct of non-state actors operating with governmental acquiescence—falls squarely within the reversible error identified in *Montejo-Gonzalez*. The agency’s decision cannot stand where, as here, it contravenes well-established precedent by imposing an impermissibly high burden of proof and inadequately addressing material evidence in the record.

The integrity of the immigration adjudicatory system depends upon the scrupulous application of the law to the facts. In this case, the Board’s decision represents a significant departure from that principle, resulting in a manifest miscarriage of justice. Mr. Gonzalez has presented credible, unrebutted testimony and substantial corroborating evidence that he was targeted by violent criminal organizations with a pattern of corrupt cooperation from Mexican authorities, establishing a clear case for protection under our laws.

Therefore, Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court grant the petition, vacate the Board’s order, and remand with instructions to grant the applications for relief, or, in the alternative, for further proceedings in which the evidence is properly evaluated under the correct legal standards.

clauses.name: Term
clauses.text: Initial term of twelve (12) months, automatically renewing for successive one-year periods unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal at least sixty (60) days prior to the end of the then-current term.

clauses.name: Service Levels
clauses.text: VendorCo shall maintain 99.9% uptime measured monthly. Downtime exceeding four (4) hours in any calendar month shall entitle ClientCorp to a service credit equal to 5% of the monthly fee.

clauses.name: Liability
clauses.text: Each party's aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the total amount paid by ClientCorp to VendorCo in the twelve (12) months preceding the event giving rise to liability.

clauses.name: Data Security
clauses.text: VendorCo shall implement commercially reasonable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to protect ClientCorp Data.

clauses.name: Indemnification
clauses.text: VendorCo shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless ClientCorp from any third-party claim arising from VendorCo's breach of its data security obligations.
